newsitem.title: FINLAND: Sweden EMU 'no' not seen priced in markka bonds.
newsitem.headline: Sweden EMU 'no' not seen priced in markka bonds.

text.p: Economists see scant impact on Finnish bonds if, as widely expected, Sweden decides for now to stay out of the first wave of Europe's single currency -- but they warn a firm Swedish "no" may still jolt the market.

"It has been discounted for a while that Finland is included in the first group of (EMU countries) and Sweden will opt for a time-out," said Esko Torsti, economist at S-E Banken in Helsinki on Tuesday. Sweden is due to announce its decision at 1430 GMT today.

"As Finland is viewed among the core EMU countries, it is more affected by the overall sentiment around the EMU question," he added. In forex, even this is having less impact than actual currency flows in the relatively illiquid markka, traders say.
Most operators expect Stockholm to give only a vague "no" to EMU, saying that would be the only rational way to keep its options open.
"It looks now as if Sweden was wise not to get involved in the EMU hassle," said Teppo Koivisto, analyst at OKOBANK, referring to current German and French upsets.
But market operators say the Finnish reaction will depend on how strong any Swedish "no" is.

There is speculation that an outright decision not to join the single currency by the current government could postpone economic and monetary union membership for one of Finland's key export rivals until 2003, after elections in 2002.

"That would be extremely negative... we are still competing in the same export markets and if Sweden remains outside for several years they will eventually gain a clear competitive edge through the currency," said one trader, requesting anonymity.

Finnish forestry lobbies in particular have voiced concern over the industry's competitiveness if their main rival chose to remain outside the single currency, insisting the pro-EMU Finnish government has underestimated the difficulties.
Esa Harmala, head of the farmers and forest owners lobby MTK, repeated in Tuesday's Helsingin Sanomat that Sweden would gain great benefit in the sawn timber industry by staying out.
"The fact is that the euro currency will not adjust to external shocks as easily as a currency remaining outside," another trader said.
He said a firm "no" from Sweden could widen the Finnish - German bond yield gap to up to 50 basis points from around 34 basis points on Tuesday.

Most experts agree that regardless of the impact of Sweden's decision on markets, a "no" will raise a heated political debate in Finland: the opposition Centre Party says it may back Finland joining, but a key condition is that Sweden goes in too.
But few believe Social Democrat Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen's coalition, which has a 141-seat majority in the 200-seat house, would be seriously threatened by increasing EMU opposition.
"The government has been so committed to the EMU process that it can't and won't change course," said Petteri Hirvonen, economist at Protos Stockbrokers.
